$comment: V-13: Scala and Rust must agree on canonicalization and the content hash.
These two things are the join key for the whole library (architecture doc
section 4), and they are the one contract written twice in two languages.
This file is the specification; both sides assert against it.
SHA-256 over the file's BYTES. Not over decoded text: two processes can
agree on bytes without first agreeing on an encoding and a line-ending

contentHashes.name: empty
contentHashes.why: an empty file still has an identity; a missing file has none

contentHashes.name: crlf
contentHashes.why: V-04: the same text with CRLF is a DIFFERENT document, which is why writing LF into a CRLF file would change its identity without changing what the user typed

contentHashes.name: no-trailing-newline
contentHashes.why: a final newline is part of the bytes, so it is part of the identity

contentHashes.name: non-ascii
contentHashes.why: V-16: Windows decodes as windows-1252 by default, which would give these bytes a different hash on one platform with no edit having occurred

contentHashes.name: emoji-astral
contentHashes.why: a surrogate pair in Java, four UTF-8 bytes on the wire; the hash is over the bytes, so the two agree

contentHashes.name: bom
contentHashes.why: a BOM is content, not metadata: it changes the bytes and therefore the identity

contentHashes.name: lone-cr
contentHashes.why: a bare CR is neither LF nor CRLF and must not be normalized away

contentHashes.name: invalid-utf8
contentHashes.why: not decodable as UTF-8; Rust's read_to_string would have replaced these bytes, silently changing the hash

contentHashes.name: nul-byte
contentHashes.why: a NUL is a legal byte in a file even where it is illegal in a path
